answers.answer: Use {target} for the name as typed, or a {target.*} helper for a detail about that person. The worked example uses {target.displayname} for the named person and {user} for the caller. The only helper on the page that takes arguments is {target.verb:<sing|plur>}, for example {target.verb:has|have}. {target.data.<key>} takes a key name. To cover the case where nobody is named, wrap the reply in the if helper with {target} as the condition.
answers.quote: {if:{target}|{user} sends a hug to {target.displayname}.|{user} sends a hug to the whole chat.}

answers.answer: You need a reply in a command, event response, pipeline or webhook; timers do not offer these helpers. The command must be used with a name after it, because the target is the first word typed after the command. The page states both in its opening paragraphs.
answers.quote: These helpers work in commands, event responses, pipelines and webhooks. A timer has no target, so they are not offered there.

answers.answer: The target is the person the reply is about, and the user is the person who used the command. It worked when the reply shows the named person's display name where {target.displayname} was. {target.known} tells a stored person (true) from one the bot has no record of (false).
answers.quote: The target is the person a reply is about when that person is not the one who used it.

answers.answer: With !hug @someone, the target is someone, so {target.displayname} shows someone's display name. If the bot has never seen them, the name comes from Twitch, or the word as typed if no account has that name. With !hug alone there is no target: the bot does not use the caller in its place. {target} and {target.displayname} are empty, so the plain reply reads 'ViewerOne sends a hug to .' The if version takes its second branch instead.
answers.quote: The bot never fills in the caller when no name is given, so !hug on its own has no target at all.

answers.answer: The 'When nobody is named' list talks about 'the three message helpers' and 'the helpers that read the person's Twitch account, channel, points or channel record' before any of those helpers are introduced. I had to scroll down to the tables to see which helpers each phrase meant, then come back to the list. That cost a reread, not a wrong action. I did not have to guess at any step.
